newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania parties should back vote despite violence.
newsitem.headline: Albania parties should back vote despite violence.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky urged Albania's bickering political leaders on Thursday to abide by their pact to hold elections on Sunday and respect the results despite a resurgence of violence in the lawless south.

Vranitzky, envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) overseeing the snap general election, said President Sali Berisha and all political parties had agreed to polling stations closing early to help ensure the safety of voters and hundreds of international observers.
Asked whether Berisha's dominant Democrats and rival opposition Socialists were likely to accept the results, the former Austrian chancellor said:
"In the political contract signed on May 9th, all 10 (main) parties said they will accept the results. Should anyone deviate from this commitment, I cannot say today what our reaction will be.
"The situation is complex and the circumstances unusual...but if we had postponed the election, the situation would not have improved but deteriorated," he added.
Campaigning by the parties has been at best sporadic, with both Democrats and Socialists unable to hold rallies in areas in the grip of rival supporters and outside police or government control.

Even some soldiers in the 7,000-strong multinational protection force deployed in Albania in April following widespread violence have been told by their national capitals to stay away from certain towns and the remote countryside.

In the Adriatic port of Vlore, where a rebellion erupted in March in response to the collapse of pyramid investment schemes, daily exchanges of gunfire escalated on Thursday into more widespread violence.

Finance Minister Arben Malaj, a Socialist, narrowly escaped from a gunbattle and was forced to take shelter in a seaside hotel after rival local warlords exchanged volleys of gunfire during an election rally held in a sports hall.
A protection force statement said local Italian army commanders despatched two platoons and two armoured personnel carriers to evacuate civilians from the smouldering building.
Calm returned to Vlore later, but a candidate for an ethnic Greek party said her father was being held near the town of Gjirokaster by men demanding she withdraw from the vote.
Like most of southern Albania, Gjirokaster and Vlore are run by so-called "Salvation Committees" violently opposed to Berisha and hoping the election will force him from office.
Senior Democratic official Leonard Demi told a news conference in Tirana that the Socialists were not allowing his party to campaign in about a third of Albania.
"They (the Socialists) want an Enver Hoxha-style campaign there...their extremism has gone so far, I wouldn't know what campaign we could mount in these conditions," he said.
Stalinist dictator Hoxha ruled Albania from 1944 until his death in 1985. Communism was toppled in Albania in late 1990.
Socialists too are barred from certain areas, and claim the Democrats fear losing power and accuse them of rigging last year's general election, which was declared flawed by the OSCE.

Nearly 500 international observers, including 112 parliamentarians from 22 countries, were to fan out around the country on Friday to prepare for the first round of the election on Sunday. OSCE officials said they would attempt to monitor polling in nearly half the 4,525 polling stations.
The constitutional court still had to rule on whether stations can close by 6 p.m. but if it could not, Vranitzky said the central electoral commission would decide to do so anyway.
The OSCE was expected to give an early verdict on the process by late Monday and first results could come a day later.
